Well, I finally got around to doing some tests I have been meaning to do for a while. As I can only get Type B Bone gelatin at max 250 bloom I wanted to try Type B Hide 275 and Type A 275.

Both batches came out cloudy after setting and drying. The only difference was I used KDi instead of AmDi which I do not think would cause the cloudiness. I didn't even attempt holograms with them because I thought the cloudiness was too much. I have never seen this with bone 250, 225 or 200.

Has anyone played with Type B Hide or Type A gelatin and/or a higher bloom gelatin? I ask because I would like to verify it was the type and bloom rather then some freak of nature last night.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: I have used hide gelatin many times, but only seen a hazyness once after drying. This was when I had mixed the gelatin with too high concentration of chemicals. When the plate dried, one of the chemicals (Borax) crystallized. The mini crystals were what caused the haze.

Yes, I believe they were made the same way.

200:21:2.5

Near 10% gel and just over 1% AmDi.

I believe bloom plays a factor depending on the time you use the freshly coated gelatin. In other words, I believe 150 bloom and 275 bloom act differently up to a certain period of curing time (~12 - 16 hours) where they then begin to behave the same. 

I am still trying to get to the full understanding of Bloom. So far what I understand is a lower bloom is softer after a period of time (17 hours). Higher bloom is harder after that same amount of time. Thus I believe this will alter the behavior of the gelatin in different temperature swelling baths prior to the 17 hour curing time.

I used KDi to try for more redder hologram.

My biggest mistake, which I always make due to the lack of time in the lab, is I want to try too much to quickly. I changed gelatin type, bloom strength and sensitiser all at the same time. A big no no.

But I believe the higher bloom acts negatively on trying for broadband hologram in which the trade off for the lower bloom is less index modulation but more wavelengths reflected thus in display holography ultimately looking brighter. I believe the lower bloom would allow easier fabrication of broadband holograms over a longer "set" time. That is, higher bloom would quickly, after say 6 - 12 - 16 hours, be harder and thus has less tendency to want to be processed for broadband. posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Two hours is on the short end, I usually shoot after 4. I am not sure what you mean by managing shrinkage. DCG is always a balance between swelling and shrinking with modifications of soak temp, alcoho temp, alcohol times and alcohol concentrations. I have always made my broadband white holograms with young film, little extra time in fixer, coolish-warm water, high temp alcohol, less alcohol baths and less time in each alcohol and sometimes flip the plate so reference is incident on emulsion side.

I guess it also has to do with film thickness and gelatin concentration in the emulsion.

I have heard of letting the plates set for a few days but I never have unless they are left over from a session. I cannot plan to be in the lab 1 or 3 days in advance. I just never know when I can make time to plan that far in advance. So I have never considered making them in advance. I make them, wait a couple/few hours, turn on the laser and let it warm up and play with the geometry, another hour or so, and shoot.

I hope this answers your question but if not, be more specific in what you would expect and I will try to tell you how I compensate.

posts.author: PAB
posts.content_md:
Well, I guess, it is because I never had the oportunity to use not completly dryed plates. My plates are always thoroughly dryed several tens of hours. So the gel is rock hard.

What I mean by the swelling is that when your plate is still wet, it contains water that will be removed in the final process. So, the gel should shrink a lot. With dry plates, you record the hologram in thinner gel and it swells during the water process but then, comes back (nearly) to its original (recording) thickness by the end of the processing.

But all that is very interesting!

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
This brings up a theory I have in the alcohol processing. It is hard to find informaton on this.

Let's say we have some gelatin and it has hardened and unhardened layers or fringes. When you put it in alcohol I belive there is a certain acohol percentage thresehold in which water has been replace with alcohol to a point that the fringes retain their RELATIVE spacing. If you nearly hit this thresehold but are just under it at a certain alcohol concentration then there is still a little water in it just under this thresehold and when the hologram is placed in the next alcohol concentration that extra water causes slight shrinkage and you get a green shifted hologram. If you nearly hit this thresehold but are just over it at a certain alcohol concentration then there is less water in it just under this thresehold and when the hologram is placed in the next alcohol concentration that lesser amount of water causes the fringes to retain or lock in slightly expaned fringes thus giving a red shifted hologram. 

In other words (this is hard to explain), at some concentration the fringes get locked. More water in this concentration more shrinkage, less water the the fringes are actually locked a little swollen.

With an older film, which is still gelatin and the gelatin alone has the capacity to absorb as much water as it could just out of the box, you get crosslinking via the dark reaction which inhibits the swell amount. Thus you may have "locked" in the fringe spacing to a degree. They don't swell as much in the water and thus the alcohol concentration thingy may not pertain as much. 

So, if I wanted my young plates to act like old plates I could simply heat them, expose them to light or some other pre-exposure hardening method.

Just some thoughts in trying to understand this living creature.
